opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's not an either/or, and the framing of "sovereignty versus globalization" can actually lead governments astray. What you really want is resilience, and resilience usually comes from diversity and redundancy rather than complete self-sufficiency.

Take medicines, which is where I've spent a lot of my time. A huge share of the active pharmaceutical ingredients for essential generic drugs, including many antibiotics, are produced in a very small number of facilities, often concentrated in one or two countries. The problem isn't that those countries are foreign. The problem is concentration. If one plant has a contamination issue, or there's an export restriction, or a lockdown like we saw during COVID, suddenly hospitals around the world are scrambling for basic drugs that cost pennies per dose. Bringing all of that production home would be enormously expensive, and frankly a single domestic plant is also a single point of failure.

So my view is that governments should first map their dependencies properly. Most don't actually know, product by product, where the critical inputs come from, sometimes several tiers down the supply chain. Once you have that picture, you can triage. For a small set of truly critical products where there's no substitute and a shortage costs lives quickly, it can make sense to maintain some domestic or regional capacity, even if it's not the cheapest option. For many others, the better tools are diversifying suppliers across friendly countries, holding strategic stockpiles, and writing procurement contracts that reward reliability and multiple sourcing rather than just the lowest price.

That last point matters a lot. We've created markets, particularly for generics and antibiotics, where the only thing buyers reward is price. That squeezes margins until only the largest, lowest-cost producers survive, and you end up with exactly the fragility you were trying to avoid. If public purchasers are willing to pay a modest premium for supply security, you can sustain more manufacturers, in more places.

And finally, I'd stress cooperation. No mid-sized country can be self-sufficient in everything. Regional arrangements, like coordinated procurement or shared reserves within a bloc of allies, let you spread the cost of resilience while avoiding the trap where everyone hoards during a crisis and makes things worse for everyone. So: sovereign capacity where it truly matters, diversified interdependence everywhere else, and markets designed to value reliability, not just cost.

r001.rationale: It says concentration is the problem regardless of whether production is foreign, and that a single domestic plant is also a single point of failure.

r002.rationale: It recommends maintaining domestic or regional capacity for a small set of critical products while diversifying suppliers across friendly countries for others.

r003.rationale: It does not propose using NATO spending commitments to fund domestic medical-countermeasure manufacturing.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that there is no single right ratio, and anyone who tells you there is probably hasn't looked closely at what happened during COVID. What we learned in 2020 and 2021 is that the problem wasn't really "we don't make enough masks domestically." The problem was that nobody had mapped where the chokepoints actually were. The UK, for instance, discovered quite late that a lot of its PPE supply chain ran through a handful of factories in a single region of China, and that the melt-blown polypropylene that goes into N95-grade masks was itself a bottleneck that almost no one had thought about. So I'd start by saying the first job of government isn't to decide between sovereignty and trade. It's to actually know its own supply chains well enough to know where that question even matters.

Once you have that map, I think the useful frame is to ask: what are the things where a disruption would be catastrophic rather than merely painful, and where the lead time to stand up production is long? Those are the cases where you want some domestic or at least allied capacity, even if it's inefficient in normal times. Antibiotics are a good example. Something like ninety percent of the active pharmaceutical ingredients for common antibiotics come from a very small number of countries, and you cannot spin up an API plant in six months. Vaccines, certain diagnostics, some medical gases, these fall into that category too. For a lot of other things, like generic consumables, the right answer is probably diversification and stockpiling rather than reshoring, because the cost of making them at home is high and the time to substitute suppliers is short.

The thing I'd push back on is the instinct to treat "sovereign manufacturing" as the goal in itself. Pure autarky is enormously expensive, it tends to produce worse products, and it has its own fragility, because if your one domestic plant has a quality failure or a fire, you've got nothing. The UK's Vaccine Manufacturing and Innovation Centre is a cautionary tale here. It was built as a sovereign capability and then sold off before it ever really did what it was designed for, partly because nobody had a clear theory of how you keep that capacity warm between crises. Capacity that only exists on paper, or that gets mothballed the moment the headlines move on, isn't sovereignty, it's theatre.

So my view is that the balance should be dynamic and layered. Strategic stockpiles for the things you can store. Standing contracts with domestic or friendly manufacturers that include surge clauses, so the capacity is exercised in peacetime and can be ramped. Deep diversification across geographies for the rest. And underneath all of it, serious investment in understanding your supply chain, including the second and third tiers, because the most dangerous dependencies are almost always the ones you didn't know you had. Governments are quite good at buying the visible thing and quite bad at funding the unglamorous mapping and maintenance work that actually makes resilience real.

r001.rationale: The response says a single domestic plant can fail and leave the country with nothing, but it does not clearly compare concentrating manufacturing within one country with having no domestic control.

r002.rationale: It recommends domestic or allied capacity for critical supplies, standing contracts with friendly manufacturers, and geographic diversification, communicating friend-shoring alongside domestic capacity.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose using the national-security portion of NATO spending to fund domestic medical-countermeasure manufacturing.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish sovereignty from self-sufficiency. You don’t necessarily need to manufacture everything within your own borders, but you do need confidence that you can obtain critical supplies when things go wrong.

For something like medical supplies, that means asking: where are the dependencies? You might have a domestic factory, but if it relies on a raw material or a component that comes from a single supplier overseas, you haven’t really resolved the vulnerability. You’ve just moved it further down the supply chain.

So I’d favour a combination of domestic capacity for particularly critical products, diversified international suppliers, and stockpiles that can bridge a disruption. The balance will depend on how essential something is, how quickly demand could rise, and how long it takes to expand production.

And international cooperation remains essential. If every country responds to a crisis by restricting exports, then relying on trade becomes much less credible. Governments need to work out those arrangements ahead of time, while also maintaining enough capacity at home that cooperation isn’t their only option.

r001.rationale: The response warns that a domestic factory can still depend on a single overseas supplier, but does not argue that concentrating all manufacturing within one country can be as fragile as having no domestic control.

r002.rationale: It recommends domestic capacity and diversified international suppliers, but does not specifically recommend extensive friend-shoring alongside partial reshoring.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention NATO spending commitments or propose using national-security funds to support domestic medical-countermeasure manufacturing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is to distinguish sovereignty from self-sufficiency. You want to be able to obtain critical supplies in a crisis, but that doesn’t necessarily mean manufacturing everything within your own borders. If your domestic factories depend on a single overseas supplier for a crucial ingredient, having the factory at home hasn’t really solved the problem.

So governments need to understand the whole supply chain: where the bottlenecks are, how concentrated production is, and how quickly you could switch suppliers or increase production. For some supplies, maintaining domestic manufacturing capacity will make sense, even if it costs more in normal times. For others, diversified international suppliers, stockpiles, and agreements with reliable partners may provide greater resilience.

And there’s a collective dimension here. If every country responds to a crisis by restricting exports, everyone can end up worse off. You need international cooperation alongside domestic preparedness. The balance I’d aim for is enough national capacity to avoid being helpless in an emergency, combined with trading relationships that don’t leave you dependent on any single country.

r001.rationale: The response says a domestic factory can remain vulnerable if it depends on a single overseas supplier, but does not state that concentrating manufacturing entirely within one country can be as fragile as having no domestic control.

r002.rationale: It recommends domestic capacity for some supplies alongside diversified international suppliers and agreements with reliable partners, conveying partner-based sourcing as a complement to partial reshoring.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose funding domestic medical-countermeasure manufacturing through NATO-related national-security spending.
